## Proof

**Claim.** If \(k\) is a field that is finitely generated as a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra, then \(k\) is finite.

*Proof.* Since \(k\) is a finitely generated \(\mathbb{Z}\)-algebra, write \(k \cong \mathbb{Z}[t_1,\dots,t_n]/\mathfrak{m}\) for a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\). Let \(\varphi:\mathbb{Z}\to k\) be the natural map. Its kernel is a prime ideal of \(\mathbb{Z}\), hence is either \((0)\) or \((p)\) for a rational prime \(p\).

---

**Case 1: \(\ker\varphi=(p)\).** Then \(k\) is a field of characteristic \(p\) and is a finitely generated \(\mathbb{F}_p\)-algebra. By **Zariski's lemma** (a field that is finitely generated as an algebra over a field is a finite algebraic extension of that field), \(k\) is a finite extension of \(\mathbb{F}_p\). Hence \(k\cong\mathbb{F}_{p^r}\) for some \(r\ge 1\), and \(k\) is finite.

---

**Case 2: \(\ker\varphi=(0)\).** Then \(\mathbb{Z}\hookrightarrow k\), so \(k\) has characteristic \(0\). Since \(k\) is a field containing \(\mathbb{Z}\), it contains the fraction field \(\mathbb{Q}\) of \(\mathbb{Z}\). Writing \(k=\mathbb{Z}[a_1,\dots,a_n]\), every element of \(k\) is a polynomial in the \(a_i\) with integer coefficients; integer coefficients are in particular rational, so
\[
k=\mathbb{Z}[a_1,\dots,a_n]\subseteq\mathbb{Q}[a_1,\dots,a_n]\subseteq k,
\]
hence \(k=\mathbb{Q}[a_1,\dots,a_n]\) is a finitely generated \(\mathbb{Q}\)-algebra. By Zariski's lemma again, \(k\) is a finite algebraic extension of \(\mathbb{Q}\), i.e. \(k\) is a number field of degree \(d=[k:\mathbb{Q}]\).

We now show this is impossible. Let \(\mathcal{O}_k\) be the ring of integers of \(k\); it is a free \(\mathbb{Z}\)-module of rank \(d\) and \(\mathcal{O}_k\otimes_{\mathbb{Z}}\mathbb{Q}=k\), so every element of \(k\) can be written as \(x/m\) with \(x\in\mathcal{O}_k\) and \(m\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\). In particular each generator \(a_i=x_i/m_i\) with \(x_i\in\mathcal{O}_k\), \(m_i\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}\). Setting \(m=m_1\cdots m_n\), we get \(a_i\in\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\) for all \(i\), hence
\[
k=\mathbb{Z}[a_1,\dots,a_n]\subseteq\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\subseteq k,
\]
so \(k=\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\).

But \(\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\) is **not** a field. Indeed, \(\mathcal{O}_k\) is integral over \(\mathbb{Z}\), so by the lying-over theorem, for every rational prime \(p\) there exists a prime ideal \(\mathfrak{P}\subset\mathcal{O}_k\) lying over \((p)\), i.e. \(\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}=(p)\). Choose a rational prime \(p\nmid m\) (possible since \(m\) has only finitely many prime divisors). Then \(m\notin\mathfrak{P}\) (otherwise \(m\in\mathfrak{P}\cap\mathbb{Z}=(p)\), forcing \(p\mid m\), a contradiction). Thus \(\mathfrak{P}\) survives in the localization \(\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\) as a nonzero prime ideal, so \(\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\) is not a field. This contradicts \(k=\mathcal{O}_k[1/m]\) being a field.

Therefore Case 2 cannot occur.

---

Since only Case 1 is possible, \(k\) is a finite field. \(\blacksquare\)
